modules.title: TypeScript for React
modules.goal: Type props, state, events, refs, context and API responses in a React app.
learn: Only the TypeScript React needs: type vs interface, unions ('idle' | 'loading' | 'error'), optional fields, arrays, and enough generics to read useState<User | null>(null).
Type props (with children: React.ReactNode), events (React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>), refs (useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null)), context and API responses.
Extend native elements: type ButtonProps = React.ComponentProps<'button'> & { variant: 'primary' | 'ghost' }.
Model UI states with discriminated unions so "loading and error at once" can't happen.

modules.title: TypeScript on Node.js
modules.goal: Run a typed Express API with Node’s built-in type stripping and keep tsc as the type checker.

build.title: Typed API
checklist: Convert the project to TypeScript with strict: true; run it with Node's built-in type stripping, and add tsc --noEmit to npm test (set erasableSyntaxOnly in tsconfig, so skip enum and namespace)

topics.title: Types and interfaces
topics.why: The everyday vocabulary of every TypeScript codebase.
topics.summary: Describe the shape of your data with annotations, object types and interfaces, so the editor and tsc catch mistakes before the code runs.
objectives: Annotate parameters and return values, and let inference handle the rest
Describe objects with `interface` or `type`, including optional and `readonly` properties
Choose between `type` and `interface`, and read the errors tsc gives you

examples.title: Annotations and inference
examples.takeaway: Only the parameters needed annotating; TypeScript inferred the rest, and still caught both mistakes.

examples.title: An interface for data from an API
examples.takeaway: `?` makes TypeScript check that `address` exists before it is used, and `readonly` stops the id from being overwritten.

examples.title: type or interface?
examples.takeaway: For object shapes either works; only a type alias can name a union such as `string | number`.

resources.note: The official tour of the types you use every day, from primitives to unions.
Optional and readonly properties, extending types, and index signatures.
Free interactive exercises that run in your editor.

topics.title: Unions and literal types
topics.why: Model values that can be one of a few shapes, such as ‘idle’ | ‘loading’ | ‘error’.
topics.summary: Say exactly which values are allowed: unions for “this or that”, literal types for fixed strings, and as const to derive them from data.
objectives: Write union types such as `string | number`, and unions of literals such as `'sm' | 'md' | 'lg'`
Derive a union from an array with `as const`, so the list and the type never drift apart
Handle `null` and `undefined` explicitly when `strict` is on

examples.title: Literal unions instead of magic strings
examples.takeaway: The allowed values show up in autocomplete, and a typo such as `'danger'` is caught before it becomes an unstyled button.

examples.title: Derive the type from the data
examples.takeaway: The array is the single source of truth: add a role to it and `Role` follows, and `isRole` checks strings from outside against the same list.

examples.title: null is part of the type
examples.takeaway: `User | null` makes the missing case visible, and TypeScript refuses to read `user.name` until it is handled.

resources.note: Read its sections on union types and literal types.
How `(typeof SIZES)[number]` turns an array’s elements into a union.
Exercises on unions and literal types, among others.

topics.title: Narrowing
topics.why: How TypeScript follows your checks so unions become safe to use.
topics.summary: Turn a union into the one type you need with typeof, instanceof, in, equality and truthiness checks, and write your own type guards.
objectives: Narrow unions with `typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`, equality and truthiness checks
Write a type guard (`value is Type`) for data you can’t trust, such as JSON
Use `never` so the compiler checks that every case is handled

examples.title: One check per type
examples.takeaway: Each early return removes one member of the union, so by the last line only `string` is left.

examples.title: Telling object shapes apart with in
examples.takeaway: `'radius' in shape` is a runtime check that TypeScript also reads as a type check.

examples.title: A type guard for data from an API
examples.takeaway: The data starts as `unknown` and becomes a `User` only after the guard has checked every field it relies on.

resources.note: Every narrowing check, type predicates, discriminated unions and `never`, in one page.
Exercises that practise narrowing in realistic code.
When a type guard grows long, a Zod schema writes the checks and the type for you.

topics.title: Reading generics
topics.why: Enough generics to read library types such as useState<User | null>(null).
topics.summary: Read and write generics: type parameters that let one function or type work with many types while keeping them connected.
objectives: Read generic types such as `useState<User | null>(null)`, `Promise<Response>` and `Record<string, number>`
Write a generic function whose return type follows its arguments, like `first<T>`
Constrain a type parameter with `extends`, and use `keyof` to accept only real property names

examples.title: A generic function
examples.takeaway: TypeScript infers `T` from each call, so the same function returns a `number` for numbers and a `string` for strings.

examples.title: Generics in React: useState
examples.takeaway: Pass the type yourself when the starting value can’t describe the state; otherwise let inference work.

examples.title: Constraining a key with keyof
examples.takeaway: `K extends keyof T` accepts only property names that exist, so a misspelt key is a compile error instead of a silent no-op.

resources.note: Type parameters, constraints and generic types, from first principles.
How `T[K]` looks up a property’s type.
How the React types use generics, from `useState` to event handlers.

topics.title: Typing props, state and events
topics.why: Standard on most professional React codebases.

topics.title: Typing API responses
topics.why: Types at the edge of the app, where data arrives from the network.

topics.title: Discriminated unions for UI state
topics.why: Make impossible states, like loading and error at once, unrepresentable.
topics.summary: Model data that arrives over time as a union of tagged states, so impossible combinations like “loading with an error” can’t even be written.
objectives: Replace separate `isLoading`, `error` and `data` fields with one discriminated union
Narrow on the tag with `if` and `switch`, in functions and in JSX
Add a `never` check, so adding a state shows every place that must handle it

examples.title: From flags to a union
examples.takeaway: The flags accept a meaningless state without complaint; the union rejects it at compile time.

examples.title: One case per state in JSX
examples.takeaway: `request.users` and `request.message` are only readable in the cases where they exist.

examples.title: A reducer with an exhaustive check
examples.takeaway: Actions are a discriminated union too, and the `never` line turns a forgotten case into a compile error.

resources.note: Read its sections on discriminated unions and exhaustiveness checking.
The argument for status values instead of booleans, with a React example.
Typing `useState` and `useReducer` with unions like these.
